title: Socinians on Philippians 2:13
source_text: LXXXVIII. Quod si quis dicat ipsum velle nostrum, non minus quam opus externum, quum de salutari bono quaestio est, Deo in Scriptura tribui, juxta illud Pauli ad Philippenses. Deus est qui operatur in vobis & velle & perficere pro bona voluntate: Respondent istis verbis & similibus quibus Deo tribuitur hominis conversio, non significari Deum omnino & necessario in hominibus efficere quod verba sonant: sed Deum nihil eorum omittere quae ad id efficiendum, libertate voluntatis nostrae salva, pertineant. Nimirum quia Deus nos ad bonum volendum allicit & invitat beneficiorum magnitudine, & promissionum tum certitudine, tum summa praestantia atque amplitudine, quibus efficit, non ut velle possimus, quod nobis naturaliter inest, sed ut reipsa velimus: quod tamen efficit ea ratione, ut semper in nostra potestate situm sit efficaciae isti divinae resistere. Quae pluribus diducta videre est apud Volkelium Socinianum, De vera Religione libro quinto capite decimo octavo.
pass_a_gloss: LXXXVIII. But if anyone says that our willing itself, no less than the external work, when the question is about saving good, is attributed in Scripture to God, according to that saying of Paul to the Philippians. It is God who works in you both to will & to accomplish according to his good pleasure: They answer that by these words & similar ones by which the conversion of man is attributed to God, it is not signified that God altogether & necessarily effects in men what the words sound: but that God omits none of those things which pertain to effecting it, the freedom of our will remaining safe. Namely because God entices & invites us to will the good by the greatness of his benefits, & by both the certainty, and the highest excellence and amplitude of his promises, by which he brings it about, not that we can will, which is in us naturally, but that we actually will: which yet he brings about in such a way, that it is always placed in our power to resist that divine efficacy. Which may be seen set out more fully in Volkelius the Socinian, On true Religion book five chapter eighteen.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXXXVIII. Someone may say that where saving good is concerned Scripture ascribes to God our very willing, no less than the outward deed, as in Paul's words to the Philippians: 'It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure.'

They answer that these words, and others like them that ascribe a person's conversion to God, do not mean that God wholly and necessarily brings about in people what the words say, but that God leaves out nothing that serves to bring it about while our will's freedom stays intact.

God draws and invites us to will the good by the greatness of his gifts and by the certainty, surpassing worth and breadth of his promises. By these he makes us not able to will, which we have by nature, but actually willing; yet he does it in such a way that it always lies in our power to resist that divine efficacy. This is set out more fully in Volkelius the Socinian, On True Religion, book 5, chapter 18.
